'''Nina Grace Jablonski'''<ref name="PhD">{{cite thesis |last=Jablonski |first=Nina Grace |date=June 29, 1981 |title=Functional Analysis of the Masticatory Apparatus of ''Theropithecus gelada'' (Primates: Cercopithecidae) |url=https://www.proquest.com/openview/c86e4395f620b019c968c673347ac629/1 |degree=PhD |publisher=University of Washington}}</ref> (born August 20, 1953)<ref name="LOC">[https://id.loc.gov/authorities/names/n92036686.html Jablonski, Nina G.]" at [[Library of Congress Linked Data Service]].</ref><ref name="NY Times 2007">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/09/science/09conv.html |title=A Conversation With Nina G. Jablonski: Always Revealing, Human Skin Is an Anthropologist's Map |work=[[The New York Times]] | first=Claudia |last=Dreifus |date=January 9, 2007 |quote=Jablonski … 53}}</ref> is an American [[anthropologist]] and [[palaeobiology|palaeobiologist]], known for her research into the evolution of [[Human skin color|skin color]] in humans. She is engaged in public education about [[human evolution]], human diversity, and [[racism]]. In 2021, she was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences|U.S. National Academy of Sciences]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=2021 NAS Election|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210426172730/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 26, 2021|access-date=2021-08-05|website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref> and in 2009, she was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=nina+jablonski&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=2021-04-23|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> She is an [[Evan Pugh]] University Professor at [[The Pennsylvania State University]], and the author of the books ''Skin: A Natural History'',<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=Jablonski|first=Nina G|title=Skin: a natural history|date=2006|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=978-0-520-24281-4|location=Berkeley|language=English|oclc=804311916}}</ref> ''Living Color: The Biological and Social Meaning of Skin Color'',<ref name=":5">{{Cite book|last=Jablonski|first=Nina G|title=Living color: the biological and social meaning of skin color|date=2014|publisher=Univ. of California Press|isbn=978-0-520-28386-2|location=Berkeley|language=English|oclc=915663938}}</ref> and the co-author (with [[Sindiwe Magona]] and [[Lynn Fellman]]) of ''Skin We Are In''.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book|last1=Magona|first1=Sindiwe|title=Skin we are in|last2=Jablonski|first2=Nina G|last3=Fellman|first3=Lynn|date=2018|publisher=David Philip Publishers |isbn=978-1-4856-2608-4|language=English|oclc=1052903822}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Jablonski grew up on a farm in upstate [[New York State]]. With encouragement from her parents, Jablonski began her exploration into the world of science when she was quite young.  She recalls exploring the nature around her home, digging for fossils near creeks and trees.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://sites.psu.edu/ninajablonski/about/|title=About {{!}} Nina Jablonski|website=sites.psu.edu|access-date=2018-11-07}}</ref> Jablonski's interest in studying human evolution stemmed from watching a [[National Geographic]] feature on the research of the famous [[Paleoanthropology|paleoanthropologists]] [[Louis Leakey]] and [[Mary Leakey]], that aired in the mid-1960s. Louis Leakey's study at [[Olduvai Gorge]] in East Africa and his focus on the [[Hominidae|hominid]] ''[[Paranthropus boisei|Zinjanthropus boisei]]'' sparked Jablonski's attention. She instantly decided that she wanted to pursue the study of human evolution, dismissing her parents' desire for her to attend medical school.<ref name=":0" />

Jablonski earned an A.B. degree in biology from [[Bryn Mawr College]] in 1975. In the same year, she enrolled in the PhD program in the Department of Anthropology at the [[University of Washington]]. Working under the primary supervision of paleoanthropologist [https://anthropology.washington.edu/people/gerald-g-eck Gerald Eck], she became interested in the evolution of the African [[Old World monkey]]s and completed her PhD in anthropology in 1981 with the dissertation, "Functional Analysis of the Masticatory Apparatus of ''[[Gelada|Theropithecus gelada]]'' (Primates: [[Old World monkey|Cercopithecidae]])."<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Functional analysis of the masticatory apparatus of Theropithecus gelada (Primates:Cercopithecidae)|date=1981|language=English|first=Nina G|last=Jablonski|oclc = 7824221}}</ref> She has continued to research the evolution of the Old World monkeys and other Old World [[primate]]s, including [[tarsier]]s, [[lemur]]s, and [[chimpanzee]]s, until the present day. She has held teaching positions at the [[University of Hong Kong]] and the [[University of Western Australia]]. During these years, Jablonski began her research on the evolution of human [[bipedalism]] and [[Human skin color|skin color]].<ref name="pennstate">{{cite web|title=Department of Anthropology – People|url=http://anth.la.psu.edu/people/ngj2|publisher=Penn State University|access-date=February 3, 2014}}</ref>

Jablonski is married to [https://anth.la.psu.edu/people/guc5 George Chaplin], a [[Geographic data and information|geospatial]] scientist, who is another professor as well as her research collaborator at Penn State University.<ref name="pennstate" />  She can write and speak fluently in Putonghua (Mandarin Chinese), and is also able to read in both Latin and German.<ref name="pennstate" />

==Career==
While a graduate student at the University of Washington, Jablonski conducted research at the [[University of Hong Kong]] in the Department of Anatomy.<ref name="pennstate" /> After completing her PhD, Jablonski accepted a position as lecturer in the Department of Anatomy at the University of Hong Kong. Remaining in this position from 1981 to 1990, she was able to continue her research into [[comparative anatomy]] and [[paleontology]].<ref name=":0" /> She began research in cooperation with the [[Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology]] in Beijing in 1982 and the [[Kunming Institute of Zoology]] in 1984. Her interest in the history of the East Asian paleoenvironment and the impact of environmental change on the evolution of mammals, especially primates, was spurred by her association with [[Paleobotany|paleobotanist]] Robert Orr Whyte and his wife Pauline Whyte. The Whytes had inaugurated a series of biannual meetings under the auspices of the Centre of Asian Studies at the University of Hong Kong that brought together prominent geologists and paleoenvironmental scientists from China and other East and Southeast Asian countries. Jablonski took over the organization of the paleoenvironmental conferences and the editing of the conference proceedings <ref name="pennstate" /> after the deaths of the Whytes. While in Hong Kong, Jablonski assisted the Forensic Pathology Service of the Royal Hong Kong Police in the identification of numerous unknown human remains,<ref name="pennstate" /> including the refinement of the use of photographic superimposition for the positive identification of individuals.<ref name="pennstate" /> Working in collaboration with colleagues from the Faculties of Medicine and Dentistry, Jablonski created the collection of human skeletal remains at the University of Hong Kong.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Savoldi|first1=Fabio|last2=Montalvao|first2=Carla|last3=Hui|first3=Liuling|last4=Leung|first4=Carl K.K.|last5=Jablonski|first5=Nina G.|last6=Tsoi|first6=James K.H.|last7=Bornstein|first7=Michael M.|date=2021|title=The Human Bone Collection of the Faculty of Dentistry at the University of Hong Kong: History and description of cranial and postcranial skeletal remains|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ajpa.24273|journal=American Journal of Physical Anthropology|language=en|volume=175|issue=3|pages=718–730|doi=10.1002/ajpa.24273|pmid=33772761|bibcode=2021AJPA..175..718S |s2cid=232387067|issn=0002-9483|url-access=subscription}}</ref> While still in Hong Kong, Jablonski began her research collaboration with George Chaplin on the origin of bipedalism in the human lineage; this work resulted in a series of publications in the early 1990s.

After her time in Hong Kong, Jablonski moved to Australia with her husband, George Chaplin, where she worked in the Department of Anatomy and Human Biology at the [[University of Western Australia]] from 1990 to 1994 as a Senior Lecturer. During this period, she began research on the evolution of human skin color. This research, along with her work on the evolution of human bipedalism, constituted her first forays into the study of [[human evolution]] and human diversification. She felt that the study of such topics was valuable for researchers because it showed that basic tools of comparative and historical biology could be used to deduce what probably happened in the past.<ref name=":0" />

From 1994 to 2006, she held the Irvine Chair of Anthropology at the [[California Academy of Sciences]] in [[San Francisco]]. During this time, she was recognized as a Fellow of the California Academy of Sciences and as a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref name="pennstate" /> Her responsibilities at the California Academy of Sciences included organization of the Wattis Symposia in Anthropology and publication of the edited proceedings of those symposia. Among the Wattis Symposium volumes she edited was ''The First Americans: The Pleistocene Colonization of the New World'',<ref>{{Cite book|last=Jablonski|first=Nina G|title=The first Americans: the Pleistocene colonization of the New World|date=2002|publisher=The California Academy of Sciences|isbn=978-0-940228-50-4|location=San Francisco, California|language=English|oclc=929655159}}</ref> which included important contributions about the nature and timing of human movements into the Americas.

After leaving the California Academy of Sciences, she moved to [[Pennsylvania State University|The Pennsylvania State University]], where she served as head of the [https://anth.la.psu.edu/ Anthropology Department] from 2006 to 2011. She is currently an Evan Pugh Professor of Anthropology at Penn State.<ref name="pennstate" /> Jablonski's research at Penn State has focused on the evolution of Old World monkeys, primate [[thermoregulation]], and the evolution and meanings of human skin pigmentation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://sites.psu.edu/ninajablonski/research/|title=Research {{!}} Nina Jablonski|website=sites.psu.edu|access-date=2018-11-07}}</ref> Starting in 2012, in partnership with [[Henry Louis Gates Jr.|Henry Louis Gates, Jr.]], host of the [[PBS]] show [[Finding Your Roots]], she led the development of a curriculum aimed at getting younger students of color more interested in [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Finding Your Roots Curriculum {{!}} Nina Jablonski|url=https://sites.psu.edu/ninajablonski/finding-your-roots/|access-date=2021-08-05|website=sites.psu.edu|language=en-US}}</ref> A series of PBS webisodes, "[https://fyrclassroom.org/ Finding Your Roots: The Seedlings]" was released in 2017 and 2018<ref>{{Cite web|title=Finding Your Roots - The Seedlings|url=http://fyrclassroom.org/|access-date=2021-08-05|website=fyrclassroom.org|language=en}}</ref> with three of the episodes earning Mid-Atlantic Emmy Awards in 2018<ref>{{Cite web|title="Finding Your Roots: The Seedlings" wins two 2018 Mid-Atlantic Emmy awards {{!}} Penn State University|url=https://news.psu.edu/photo/541631/2018/10/15/finding-your-roots-seedlings-wins-two-2018-mid-atlantic-emmy-awards|access-date=2021-08-05|website=news.psu.edu|language=en|archive-date=August 5, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210805200540/https://news.psu.edu/photo/541631/2018/10/15/finding-your-roots-seedlings-wins-two-2018-mid-atlantic-emmy-awards|url-status=dead}}</ref> and 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210426172730/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 26, 2021|title=News from the National Academy of Sciences|date=April 26, 2021|access-date=July 4, 2021|quote=Newly elected members and their affiliations at the time of election are:  ...  Jablonski, Nina G.; Evan Pugh University Professor, department of anthropology, Pennsylvania State University, University Park}}, entry in member directory:{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/nina-g-jablonski-0efb6d/|title=Member Directory|access-date=2021-07-04|publisher=National Academy of Sciences}}</ref>

==Research==
Jablonski researches [[Human evolution|human]] and [[Evolution of primates|primate evolution]].<ref name = pennstate /> She is known for her research into human skin, and has published two books on the subject. She researches the origin and evolution of the skin and [[Human skin color|skin pigmentation]] and the relationships between [[vitamin D]] requirements and metabolism in the context of [[human migration]] and [[urbanization]].<ref name = pennstate /> In 2012 she was awarded a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] to carry out research into human vitamin D production in natural conditions with the goal of informing public health interventions addressing [[vitamin D deficiency]].<ref name=Guggenheim>{{cite web |title=Fellows: Nina G Jablonski |url=http://www.gf.org/fellows/17236-nina-g-jablonski |publisher=Guggenheim Fellowship |access-date=February 8, 2014 |archive-date=February 22, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222091922/http://www.gf.org/fellows/17236-nina-g-jablonski |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Skin color ===
Jablonski studies the physiological functions of skin as well as the evolutionary and sociological influences of the past and today. Early in her skin research, she published papers on the connection between [[neural tube defect]]s and [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet radiation]], which damages [[folate]] in the skin, in the controversial and non-[[peer review]]ed journal ''[[Medical Hypotheses]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Jablonski|first=N.G.|date=June 1999|title=A possible link between neural tube defects and ultraviolet light exposure|journal=Medical Hypotheses|volume=52|issue=6|pages=581–582|doi=10.1054/mehy.1997.0697|pmid=10459842|issn=0306-9877}}</ref> This research was put on a strong empirical footing when she, in collaboration with George Chaplin, examined the measured skin color of indigenous human populations relative to levels of ultraviolet radiation at the earth's surface as measured by the [[NASA]] [[Total Ozone Mapping Spectrometer|TOMS 7 satellite]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chaplin|first1=George|last2=Jablonski|first2=Nina G.|date=1998-10-01|title=Hemispheric difference in human skin color|journal=American Journal of Physical Anthropology|volume=107|issue=2|pages=221–223|doi=10.1002/(sici)1096-8644(199810)107:2<221::aid-ajpa8>3.0.co;2-x|pmid=9786336|issn=1096-8644}}</ref> In their paper on the evolution of human skin pigmentation, Jablonski and Chaplin also posited that dark skin with [[sweat gland]]s evolved with the loss of most body hair, and demonstrated that [[sexual dimorphism]] in skin color was nearly universal in humans (with females tending towards lighter skin than males).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jablonski|first1=N. G.|last2=Chaplin|first2=G.|date=July 2000|title=The evolution of human skin coloration|journal=Journal of Human Evolution|volume=39|issue=1|pages=57–106|doi=10.1006/jhev.2000.0403|issn=0047-2484|pmid=10896812 |bibcode=2000JHumE..39...57J }}</ref> They also speculated that similar skin colors evolved independently in different human populations under similar solar regimes, an insight that preceded the [[Molecular genetics|molecular genetic]] studies that confirmed the phenomenon. Jablonski's major findings explain that the physiological purpose for the variation in skin color around the world is due to the balance between the need to protect against ultraviolet radiation and facilitating the production of [[vitamin D]]. Darker skin due to increased [[Melanin|eumelanin]] levels occurs in populations closer to the equator where ultraviolet radiation poses risks of [[folate]] damage, and [[depigmentation]] occurs in areas with low and highly seasonal levels of ultraviolet radiation so that vitamin D biosynthesis is not inhibited.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Jablonski|first1=Nina G.|last2=Chaplin|first2=George|date=October 2002|title=Skin Deep|journal=Scientific American|volume=287|issue=4|pages=74–81|doi=10.1038/scientificamerican1002-74|pmid=12271527|bibcode=2002SciAm.287d..74J|issn=0036-8733}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jablonski|first1=Nina G.|last2=Chaplin|first2=George|date=2010-05-11|title=Human skin pigmentation as an adaptation to UV radiation|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=107|issue=Supplement 2|pages=8962–8968|doi=10.1073/pnas.0914628107|issn=0027-8424|pmc=3024016|pmid=20445093|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Jablonski|first=Nina G.|date=October 2004|title=The Evolution of Human Skin and Skin Color|journal=Annual Review of Anthropology|volume=33|issue=1|pages=585–623|doi=10.1146/annurev.anthro.33.070203.143955|issn=0084-6570}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chaplin|first1=George|last2=Jablonski|first2=Nina G.|date=August 2009|title=Vitamin D and the evolution of human depigmentation|journal=American Journal of Physical Anthropology|volume=139|issue=4|pages=451–461|doi=10.1002/ajpa.21079|pmid=19425101|bibcode=2009AJPA..139..451C |issn=0002-9483}}</ref> Jablonski's recent collaboration with [[Physiology|physiologists]] [https://hhd.psu.edu/contact/w-kenney-phd W. Larry Kenney] and Tony Wolf at Penn State has yielded new research indicating a probable link between UV-induced folate loss and impaired thermoregulation.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wolf|first1=S. Tony|last2=Stanhewicz|first2=Anna E.|last3=Jablonski|first3=Nina G.|last4=Kenney|first4=W. Larry|date=2018-10-01|title=Acute ultraviolet radiation exposure attenuates nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation in the cutaneous microvasculature of healthy humans|journal=Journal of Applied Physiology|language=en|volume=125|issue=4|pages=1232–1237|doi=10.1152/japplphysiol.00501.2018|issn=8750-7587|pmc=6230571|pmid=30138076}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wolf|first1=S. Tony|last2=Jablonski|first2=Nina G.|last3=Ferguson|first3=Sara B.|last4=Alexander|first4=Lacy M.|last5=Kenney|first5=W. Larry|date=2020-10-01|title=Four weeks of vitamin D supplementation improves nitric oxide-mediated microvascular function in college-aged African Americans|journal=American Journal of Physiology. Heart and Circulatory Physiology|language=en|volume=319|issue=4|pages=H906–H914|doi=10.1152/ajpheart.00631.2020|issn=0363-6135|pmc=7654656|pmid=32857616}}</ref>

Jablonski has taken this connection and applied it to understanding the effects of modern lifestyles on human health. Jablonski connects certain diseases and health risks to people living in areas distant from those of their ancestors and to people who are living the modern indoors lifestyle.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Jablonski|first=Ng|date=2012-03-16|title=The evolution of human skin colouration and its relevance to health in the modern world|url=http://www.rcpe.ac.uk/journal/issue/journal_42_1/jablonsky.pdf|journal=The Journal of the Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh|volume=42|issue=1|pages=58–63|doi=10.4997/JRCPE.2012.114|pmid=22441067|doi-access=free}}{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref name=":3" /> Vitamin D deficiency is linked directly to several serious diseases including [[rickets]], and is implicated in the causality of [[multiple sclerosis]] and many malignancies.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Jablonski|first1=Nina G.|last2=Chaplin|first2=George|date=2012-03-19|title=Human skin pigmentation, migration and disease susceptibility|journal=Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B|volume=367|issue=1590|pages=785–792|doi=10.1098/rstb.2011.0308|issn=0962-8436|pmc=3267121|pmid=22312045}}</ref> The main health problems related to too much UV radiation are [[skin cancer]]s, the most serious and rare being cutaneous [[melanoma]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Melanoma|url=https://www.skincancer.org/skin-cancer-information/melanoma/|access-date=2021-08-05|website=The Skin Cancer Foundation|language=en-US}}</ref> Birth defects due to [[folate deficiency]] are well known, but those tied directly to the effects of UVR-induced folate loss have not been documented in modern people.

=== Skin color and concepts of race ===
Since 2010, Jablonski has focused much of her research on understanding the link between skin color and the creation of color-based [[Race (human categorization)|races]] during the [[Age of Enlightenment|European Enlightenment]].<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Jablonski|first=Nina G.|date=2012|title=The struggle to overcome racism|url=https://doi.org/10.1016/S0262-4079(12)62264-7|journal=New Scientist|language=en|volume=215|issue=2880|pages=26–29|doi=10.1016/S0262-4079(12)62264-7|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>Jablonski, N. G. (2015). The Evolution of Scientific Racism. Paper presented at the American Association for the Advancement of Science Annual Meeting, San Jose, CA.</ref>  The naming of groups of people, later referred to as races, based on skin color has proven durable because of its reinforcement by European and American business interests and politicians of the 18th century who benefited from the [[Atlantic slave trade|transatlantic slave trade]].<ref name=":5" /> Jablonski's interest in the effects of race and racism in the U.S. and South Africa led to her being invited to be a Fellow of the Stellenbosch Institute for Advanced Study (STIAS) in 2011,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nina Jablonski|url=https://stias.ac.za/fellows/nina-jablonski/|access-date=2021-08-05|website=Stellenbosch Institute for Advanced Study|language=en-US}}</ref> and to be involved in the "Effects of Race Project"<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Effects of Race |url=https://stias.ac.za/fellows/projects/effects-of-race/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928201109/https://stias.ac.za/fellows/projects/effects-of-race/ |archive-date=Sep 28, 2023 |website=Stellenbosch Institute for Advanced Study}}</ref> at STIAS from 2013 to 2020. In 2010, Jablonski received an honorary doctorate (D.Phil.) from [[Stellenbosch University]] for her contribution to the worldwide fight against racism.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2010-03-13|title=Sydney Brenner and Nina Jablonski present lectures at STIAS|url=https://stias.ac.za/2010/03/sydney-brenner-and-nina-jablonski-present-lectures-at-stias/|access-date=2021-08-05|website=Stellenbosch Institute for Advanced Study|language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Eumelanin Human Skin Colour Scale ===
Jablonski is a member of an international collaborative research group that developed the [[Eumelanin Human Skin Colour Scale]], a novel method for classifying human skin colour that is independent of race, ethnicity and ancestry.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dadzie |first1=Ophelia E. |last2=Sturm |first2=Rick A. |last3=Fajuyigbe |first3=Damilola |last4=Petit |first4=Antoine |last5=Jablonski |first5=Nina G. |date=2022 |title=The Eumelanin Human Skin Colour Scale: a proof-of-concept study |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/bjd.21277 |journal=British Journal of Dermatology |language=en |volume=187 |issue=1 |pages=99–104 |doi=10.1111/bjd.21277 |pmid=35349165 |issn=1365-2133|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=patienthub |date=2022-05-09 |title=Researchers propose new evidence-based approach to describing skin colour |url=https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/researchers-propose-new-evidence-based-approach-to-describing-skin-colour/ |access-date=2026-08-09 |website=BAD Patient Hub |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Iacobucci |first=Gareth |date=2022-05-10 |title=Researchers propose new evidence based scale for describing skin colour |url=https://www.bmj.com/content/377/bmj.o1175 |journal=BMJ |language=en |volume=377 |article-number=o1175 |doi=10.1136/bmj.o1175 |pmid=35537751 |issn=1756-1833|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Old World monkeys ===
Jablonski's research on Old World monkeys is marked by extensive paleontological field work across Africa and Asia. Her work has led to significant discoveries including an ape cranium in China,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ji|first1=XuePing|last2=Jablonski|first2=Nina G.|last3=Su|first3=Denise F.|last4=Deng|first4=ChengLong|last5=Flynn|first5=Lawrence J.|last6=You|first6=YouShan|last7=Kelley|first7=Jay|date=2013|title=Juvenile hominoid cranium from the terminal Miocene of Yunnan, China|journal=Chinese Science Bulletin|language=en|volume=58|issue=31|pages=3771–3779|doi=10.1007/s11434-013-6021-x|bibcode=2013ChSBu..58.3771J|issn=1001-6538|doi-access=free}}</ref> and the first identified chimpanzee fossils. In 2004, along with [[Sally McBrearty]], Jablonski discovered teeth in the collections of the [[National Museums of Kenya|National Museum of Kenya]] which originated from the [[Kapthurin Formation]] and dated back to ~545,000 years ago. By comparing their measurements to those of modern ''[[Pan (genus)|Pan]]'' teeth, Jablonski and McBrearty determined the fossils belonged to the genus ''Pan'' .<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=McBrearty|first1=Sally|last2=Jablonski|first2=Nina G.|date=September 2005|title=First fossil chimpanzee|journal=Nature|volume=437|issue=7055|pages=105–108|doi=10.1038/nature04008|pmid=16136135|bibcode=2005Natur.437..105M|s2cid=4423286|issn=0028-0836}}</ref> Paleoecological evidence at the site showed that chimpanzees were not restricted to forest habitats.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn7917-first-convincing-chimp-fossil-discovered/|title=First convincing chimp fossil discovered|last=Orwant|first=Robin|work=New Scientist|access-date=2018-11-07}}</ref> Along with the discovery of nearby ''[[Homo]]'' fossils of the same age, this provided the first fossil evidence for spatiotemporal coexistence between the two genera.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.livescience.com/9326-chimp-fossils.html|title=First-ever Chimp Fossils Found|work=Live Science|access-date=2018-11-07}}</ref> More recently, Jablonski's fossil discoveries have been complemented by [[Phylogenetics|phylogenetic]] analysis of modern [[ape]]s,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Carbone|first1=Lucia|last2=Alan Harris|first2=R.|last3=Gnerre|first3=Sante|last4=Veeramah|first4=Krishna R.|last5=Lorente-Galdos|first5=Belen|last6=Huddleston|first6=John|last7=Meyer|first7=Thomas J.|last8=Herrero|first8=Javier|last9=Roos|first9=Christian|date=2014-09-10|title=Gibbon genome and the fast karyotype evolution of small apes|journal=Nature|volume=513|issue=7517|pages=195–201|doi=10.1038/nature13679|issn=0028-0836|pmc=4249732|pmid=25209798|bibcode=2014Natur.513..195C}}</ref> suggesting that genomic divergence in ancestral [[gibbon]]s was in part due to habitat shifts during the [[Miocene]]–[[Pliocene]] transition.

Jablonski's research on the genus ''[[Gelada|Theropithecus]]'' also had significant impact, including the discovery of a near-complete skeleton of ''[[Theropithecus brumpti]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Jablonski|first=N|date=December 2002|title=A new skeleton of Theropithecus brumpti (Primates: Cercopithecidae) from Lomekwi, West Turkana, Kenya|journal=Journal of Human Evolution|volume=43|issue=6|pages=887–923|doi=10.1006/jhev.2002.0607|pmid=12473488|bibcode=2002JHumE..43..887J|issn=0047-2484}}</ref> This finding established ''T. brumpti'' as a terrestrial monkey similar to the modern ''[[Gelada|T. gelada]]'', albeit much larger. Her research is central to modern understanding of extinct ''Theropithecus'' size, habitat, and diet,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cerling|first1=Thure E.|last2=Chritz|first2=Kendra L.|last3=Jablonski|first3=Nina G.|last4=Leakey|first4=Meave G.|last5=Manthi|first5=Fredrick Kyalo|date=2013-06-25|title=Diet of Theropithecus from 4 to 1 Ma in Kenya|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=110|issue=26|pages=10507–10512|doi=10.1073/pnas.1222571110|issn=0027-8424|pmc=3696767|pmid=23733967|bibcode=2013PNAS..11010507C|doi-access=free}}</ref> much of which is detailed in ''Theropithecus: The Rise and Fall of a Primate Genus'', edited by Jablonski. She has also written textbook analyses of the fossil record of tarsiers,<ref>Jablonski, N. G. (2003). The evolution of the tarsiid niche. In P. C. Wright, E. L. Simons, & S. Gursky (Eds.), Tarsiers:  Past, Present, and Future (pp. 35-49). New Brunswick: Rutgers University Press.</ref> gibbons,<ref>Jablonski, N. G., & Chaplin, G. (2009). The fossil record of gibbons. In S. Lappan & D. J. Whittaker (Eds.), The Gibbons: New Perspectives on Small Ape Socioecology and Population Biology (pp. 111-130). New York: Springer.{{Cite book|url=https://www.springer.com/us/book/9780387886039|title=The Gibbons - New Perspectives on Small Ape Socioecology and Population Biology {{!}} Susan Lappan {{!}} Springer|publisher=Springer|year=2009|isbn=9780387886039|series=Developments in Primatology: Progress and Prospects|doi=10.1007/978-0-387-88604-6|editor1-last=Whittaker|editor1-first=Danielle|editor2-first=Susan|editor2-last=Lappan}}</ref> and ''[[Old World monkey|Cercopithecoidea]]'' as a whole.<ref>{{Citation|last1=Jablonski|first1=Nina G.|chapter=Cercopithecoidea|date=2010-07-20|chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1525/california/9780520257214.003.0023|title=Cenozoic Mammals of Africa|pages=393–428|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=978-0-520-25721-4|access-date=2021-08-05|last2=Frost|first2=Stephen|doi=10.1525/california/9780520257214.003.0023|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref>

=== Primate thermoregulation ===
In 1994, Jablonski argued against a theory proposed by Peter Wheeler that [[thermoregulation]] played a role in hominids’ transition to [[bipedalism]]. Wheeler hypothesized that there was evolutionary pressure for early hominids to adopt bipedalism because an upright stance with less surface area exposed to sunlight allowed them to forage for longer without overheating. Jablonski's team constructed their own models, which led to the conclusion that thermoregulatory benefits weren't significant enough for natural selection to favor bipedalism.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chaplin|first1=George|last2=Jablonski|first2=Nina G.|last3=Cable|first3=N.Timothy|date=December 1994|title=Physiology, thermoregulation and bipedalism|journal=Journal of Human Evolution|volume=27|issue=6|pages=497–510|doi=10.1006/jhev.1994.1066|bibcode=1994JHumE..27..497C |issn=0047-2484}}</ref>

In 2014, Jablonski began researching the adaptation of [[goose bumps]] because she was interested in the connection between the [[Integumentary system|integument]] of [[ring-tailed lemur]]s and thermoregulation. The mechanism for goose bumps is the contraction of smooth muscle called Musculi Arrectores Pilorum (MAP).<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Chaplin|first1=George|last2=Jablonski|first2=Nina G.|last3=Sussman|first3=Robert W.|last4=Kelley|first4=Elizabeth A.|date=2013-10-31|title=The Role of Piloerection in Primate Thermoregulation|journal=Folia Primatologica|language=english|volume=85|issue=1|pages=1–17|doi=10.1159/000355007|pmid=24192984|issn=0015-5713|doi-access=}}</ref> Jablonski noted that early primates did not have effective networks of MAP throughout the body, a factor that may have significantly affected their ability to forage under the cooler conditions of the late [[Eocene]] epoch. Using this information, she concluded that the absence of MAP networks in early primates likely contributed to their extinction in non-tropical latitudes. Jablonski also made connections between goose bumps and brain size, as the ability to regulate body temperature without changes in metabolism seemed to her a necessary adaptation to accommodate the thermal and metabolic sensitivities of larger brains.<ref name=":4" />

Jablonski is also interested in exploring how the behaviors of ring-tailed lemurs relate to thermoregulation. In 2016, she traveled to Madagascar where she concluded that lemurs depend on behaviors of sunbathing and huddling to retain heat.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kelley|first1=Elizabeth A.|last2=Jablonski|first2=Nina G.|last3=Chaplin|first3=George|last4=Sussman|first4=Robert W.|last5=Kamilar|first5=Jason M.|date=2016-02-17|title=Behavioral thermoregulation inLemur catta: The significance of sunning and huddling behaviors|journal=American Journal of Primatology|volume=78|issue=7|pages=745–754|doi=10.1002/ajp.22538|pmid=26890578|s2cid=3799328|issn=0275-2565|doi-access=}}</ref>
